::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
The same workflow you have been running on satellite imagery, applied to a commercial question with no imagery in it at all. You will build a suitability surface for opening a minimarket, discover a data leak that produces a perfect and worthless model, and interpret the result with SHAP.
:::

## Why this chapter is in a remote sensing book

Everything up to here used raster features derived from satellites. Notice, though, that nothing in Chapters [-@sec-sampling] to [-@sec-obia] actually cared about that. The sampling design, the train and validate split, the classifier, the confusion matrix: none of it knows or needs to know that the numbers came from an orbiting sensor.

Swap reflectance for distance to the nearest school or clinic. Swap pixel for hexagon. Swap ground truth polygons for the locations of businesses that already exist. The machine is identical and the question becomes commercial.

Recognising that is worth more than either technique on its own, and practically it is what makes these skills portable. The same person who maps mangroves for a conservation NGO can build a site selection model for a retail chain without learning a new method, only a new domain.

## The problem

For a minimarket, the small convenience store that sits on almost every busy street in an Indonesian city, location is most of the business plan. The shelves, the prices and the opening hours are set by the chain; what the franchisee chooses is the corner. That choice has traditionally been made by intuition and a walk around the neighbourhood. The conventional GIS improvement on that is multi criteria decision analysis, where an analyst assigns weights to criteria by judgement and overlays them. That is better than intuition, and it still has the weights coming out of somebody's head.

The GeoAI version learns the weights from what has already happened. Instead of asserting that proximity to a school matters twice as much as the number of residents, we let a model observe where minimarkets actually stand and derive the relationship, then use SHAP to read the weights back out in a form a human can argue with.

## Building the features

Raw geometry cannot enter a model. Points, lines and polygons must become numbers attached to a consistent unit of analysis, and two decisions dominate the quality of the result.

**The unit.** Administrative districts are the obvious choice and the wrong one, because they vary enormously in size, so a count of anything is not comparable between them. A regular grid fixes it. Hexagons beat squares for two reasons: every neighbour of a hexagon is equidistant from its centre, whereas a square's diagonal neighbours are 1.41 times further away, which distorts any adjacency reasoning; and hexagons have no preferred axis, so they do not impose a north south artefact on a city whose structure runs diagonally. Uber's H3 system provides a global hierarchical hexagonal index, and resolution 9, roughly 175 metres across, matches a two minute walk.

**The feature families.** Two kinds of spatial feature answer genuinely different questions.

*Proximity* asks how far to the nearest instance. It measures accessibility.

*Density* asks how many within a radius. It measures intensity.

Both are needed. One school 300 metres away and twelve schools 300 metres away produce identical proximity values and very different footfall.

For population, the script sums the WorldPop 100 m raster into every hexagon in Earth Engine, so each hexagon carries its own count of people rather than a district average.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common failure: computing distance in degrees
Every distance operation must run in a projected coordinate system with metres as its unit. If your GeoDataFrame is in EPSG:4326 when you call `.distance()`, the result is in degrees of arc, which vary with latitude and are not metres. The code will run, the numbers will look plausible, and the model will be built on a measurement that does not exist. Reproject to the correct UTM zone first, every time.
:::

## Manufacturing a label

This is the conceptually hardest step in the chapter and the one most tutorials skip.

There is no dataset of good minimarket locations. So we assume that a place where a minimarket already trades is a place that works, and label those hexagons 1. That assumption deserves to be said out loud, because it encodes the existing market's judgement including its blind spots. A genuinely underserved neighbourhood looks like a bad location to this model, for the simple reason that nobody has opened there yet.

The absence side is worse. An empty hexagon is not a proven failure. It may be untried, or unavailable, or zoned for something else. Ecologists hit this problem long ago in species distribution modelling and gave it a name: presence and pseudo absence. The standard treatment is to sample a balanced number of unoccupied cells at random and label them 0, while remembering that they represent a typical unoccupied location rather than a known bad one.

::: {.callout-important}
## Scientific integrity: the label is an assumption, not an observation
Every conclusion from this model inherits the assumption above. When presenting the result, say so. A suitability map built on presence and pseudo absence is a map of where the location resembles places that already work, which is a useful and defensible statement, and it is not the same statement as where a new shop would succeed.
:::

## The perfect model that means nothing

Run the model with every feature and it reports a test accuracy of 0.99, an f1 of 0.99 and an out-of-bag score of 0.99, on 299 hexagons that have a minimarket and 299 that do not, out of 1,599 hexagons in Kota Bandung. In a textbook that is success. In real work it is an alarm.

The leak is obvious once seen. A presence hexagon contains a minimarket. Therefore its distance to the nearest competitor is close to zero *by construction*. The model has not learned what makes a location good. It has learned to recognise a hexagon with a minimarket in it, which is the label restated as a feature.

Remove that one variable and the scores fall: out-of-bag 0.78, test accuracy 0.75. Lower, and a real number about a real relationship. (With only 120 test hexagons, the test accuracy is itself uncertain by several points; the out-of-bag score, computed on every training hexagon, is the steadier of the two.)

::: {.callout-tip}
## From the field
Treat any classifier that reports near perfect accuracy as guilty until proven innocent. Ask, for every feature, whether it could have been observed before the label existed. If the answer is no, it is leaking. This single reflex catches more bad models than any amount of cross validation, and it applies identically to remote sensing: a mangrove classifier trained on a feature stack that includes an existing mangrove extent product will report spectacular accuracy and have learned nothing.
:::

Note which competitor feature survives. Distance to the nearest competitor leaks; count of competitors within 500 metres does not, because it describes the neighbourhood rather than the cell itself. Understanding why one leaks and the other does not is the point of the exercise.

## Reading the model with SHAP

Random Forest feature importance tells you which variables the model used. It does not tell you in which direction, and for a business decision the direction is the entire value.

SHAP decomposes each individual prediction into per feature contributions, so you learn not only that competitor density mattered but that more competitors pushed the prediction upward. In Bandung the count of minimarkets within 500 m carries 40 % of the model's weight, more than twice anything else.

That last finding is the commercially interesting one and it contradicts intuition. Clustering attracts rather than repels. Anyone who has walked an Indonesian street has seen two rival minimarkets facing each other across the road, and the model has found the same pattern in the data: where there are already several minimarkets, another one is more likely, not less. Minimarkets follow the same footfall, so the places that suit one suit its competitors too, and at this scale that agglomeration effect outweighs the competition effect. Note what the model cannot see: whether the fifth minimarket on a street is profitable or simply there. It learns where minimarkets stand, not whether they make money.

The other effects are smaller and all point the way a shopkeeper would expect. Being close to a main road comes second (18 %): a minimarket lives on passing traffic, and a hexagon far from a primary, secondary or tertiary road scores lower. More residents in the hexagon (WorldPop) raises the score (12 %), and so does being close to a school or a health facility (12 % and 11 %). The *counts* of schools and clinics within 500 m add almost nothing once the distances are known (3 % each). These directions are plausible, but plausible is not proven: the model has generated hypotheses about Bandung, and they should be checked before anyone acts on them. The weights are also local. A city with a different street pattern or a different retail history can give the same features different weights and even different directions. Never carry one city's weights to another without rerunning.

## From classification to a score

The classifier answers a binary question about a few hundred labelled cells. The business needs a continuous ranking of all of them.

You could predict class probability directly. This chapter instead uses the SHAP weights to build an explicit weighted sum, for one practical reason: a client can see exactly why a cell scored what it did, and can override a weight they disagree with on business grounds they have and you do not. An interpretable model that a decision maker will actually use beats a marginally better model they will not.

Two mechanical points matter in that calculation. Features must be normalised to a common 0 to 1 scale before weighting, or a variable measured in thousands of people per square kilometre will dominate one measured in counts. And features whose effect is negative must be inverted, so that a high normalised value always means "better". The script takes the direction from SHAP rather than assuming it: distance to the road, to schools and to health facilities are inverted, because the model found that closer is better, while population is not, because more residents raised the score. Getting a direction wrong produces a map that looks entirely plausible and recommends precisely the wrong locations.

## What the score is not

It is a structured, reproducible, interpretable ranking of locations by measurable characteristics, and it is a substantial improvement on walking around and forming an impression.

It is not a prediction of profit. It contains no rent, no lease availability, no parking, no local regulation, no competitor quality, and no knowledge of who actually walks down which street at eight in the morning. And because the strongest feature is the number of minimarkets already nearby, the score is drawn towards streets that are already crowded: in Bandung all ten of the best-scoring empty hexagons sit in the dense centre, each with between 9 and 20 minimarkets within 500 metres. Whether such a cell is an opportunity or a saturated market is exactly the question the model cannot answer. There is a data caveat too. A presence hexagon is one where somebody has *mapped* a minimarket in OpenStreetMap, and mapping is more complete in some neighbourhoods than others, so part of what the model learns is where volunteers have been.

Use it to reduce a thousand candidate locations to ten. Then send someone to stand on the corner for an hour. The model narrows the search; it does not make the decision.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Rerun at H3 resolution 8 and explain what happens to the agglomeration effect and why.
2. Redefine pseudo absence as cells more than one kilometre from any existing minimarket. Argue for or against that being a better definition than random sampling.
3. Add one feature of your own and use SHAP to decide whether it earned its place.
4. Take the ten highest scoring cells and inspect each on street level imagery. Count how many are plausible. That count is your real accuracy.
5. Map this chapter's workflow onto Chapter [-@sec-supervised] line by line. Write down which step in each corresponds to which step in the other.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

**1.** At H3 resolution 8 each hexagon is about 0.74 km² instead of about 0.1 km² at resolution 9, so each cell holds several minimarkets and their neighbourhoods. The agglomeration effect (stores cluster near other stores) weakens as a predictor, because the count of nearby stores and the label now describe the same cell: most cells near a store also contain one, and the contrast between occupied and empty cells is averaged away. Coarser cells mix the drivers you are trying to separate.

**2.** For: cells far from any store are more likely to be genuinely unattractive (or at least tried and avoided), so the 0 label is cleaner. Against: it makes the problem artificially easy, because distance to the nearest store then almost defines the label, the same leakage as the perfect model, and it removes exactly the near-but-empty cells where the decision is hardest. Random pseudo-absences are the safer default; the 1 km rule is defensible only if distance features are dropped.

**3.** Add, for example, the number of schools within 500 m or the length of main road in the cell. Compute SHAP values on the test set: keep the feature if it ranks above the median feature by mean |SHAP| and its effect has a plausible direction (more footfall, higher score). If it ranks low, or its effect is erratic in sign, it has not earned its place. Also check that it is not a disguised copy of the label.

**4.** Open each of the ten cells in Street View or a recent high-resolution image. Plausible means a road-front location with housing or footfall where a minimarket could open, not a river, a cemetery, a toll road or a military area. Typical results: six to eight of ten plausible. That count, with its reasons, says more about real performance than the 0.78 out-of-bag score.

**5.** Unit: pixel ↔ hexagon. Features: spectral bands, indices, terrain ↔ distances, counts, population. Labels: field-validated classes ↔ existing minimarkets (presence) and random cells (pseudo-absence). Split: hold-out polygons ↔ hold-out hexagons. Model: Random Forest in both. Diagnostics: feature importance ↔ SHAP, plus the leakage check. Output: a class map ↔ a suitability score map. Validation: independent field points ↔ street-level inspection.
:::
